Introduction to meddecide

Source: vignettes/01-introduction.Rmd
01-introduction.Rmd

meddecide is a jamovi module, and an R package, for the statistics of medical decisions in pathology and clinical research: how well raters agree, how accurate a diagnostic test is, where to put a cut-off, how two tests combine, whether a prediction model is clinically useful, and how many cases an agreement study needs.

What is in the module

The meddecide menu in jamovi has six groups:

Group Analyses
Agreement Interrater Reliability
Decision Medical Decision; Combine Medical Decision Tests; Compare Medical Decision Tests; Analysis Without Gold Standard
Decision Calculators Medical Decision Calculator; Co-Testing Analysis; Sequential Testing Analysis
Decision Curve Analysis Decision Curve Analysis
ROC Clinical ROC Analysis; Advanced ROC Analysis
Prediction Models LASSO Logistic Regression

Three sample-size tools for agreement studies appear under jamovi’s Power menu, in Power Analysis by meddecide: Confidence Interval Approach for the Number of Subjects Required, Power Approach for the Number of Subjects Required, and Lowest Expected Kappa for a Fixed Sample Size.

Use meddecide in R lists all 15 analyses with their R function names and links to the articles.

Installing

In jamovi: open the jamovi library (the + Modules button), find meddecide and install it. Example data sets are under File > Open > Data Library > meddecide.

In R:

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("sbalci/meddecide")
library(meddecide)

Where to start

  • Agreement between pathologists: Inter-Rater Agreement and Reliability, then Diagnostic Style Clustering.
  • Accuracy of a test against a reference standard: Diagnostic Test Evaluation.
  • Two tests together: Co-Testing and Sequential Testing.
  • No reference standard: Analysis Without a Gold Standard.
  • Cut-offs and AUC: ROC Curve Analysis.
  • Planning an agreement study: the three kappa sample-size articles.

A note on interpretation

The module reports estimates with confidence intervals and explains them in plain language, but it does not decide whether a test or a rater panel is good enough for clinical use. That depends on the clinical question, the setting and the consequences of errors, and it should be judged on the confidence interval, not on the point estimate alone.

Choosing and interpreting an analysis explains prevalence, dependence, validation and the different kappa planning targets.
